source.title: Towards Scaling Laws for Symbolic Regression
source.authors: Dave Otte; J. Franke; A. Zela; Fabio Ferreira; Frank Hutter

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies scaling-law analysis to transformer-based symbolic regression, a different task setting from language-model pretraining, and reports its own scaling results.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own validation-loss, solved-rate, and compute-optimal allocation results. References to language-model scaling papers are background, not catalogued results. Hyperparameter-grid details are not recorded as separate findings here.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own encoder-decoder transformers for symbolic regression, a non-language task, from 6.5M to 93M parameters over about three orders of compute. It fits power laws to the Pareto front for validation loss, solved rate and compute-optimal parameter and token counts. These results bear on V5, the power-law form outside text, and on V3, compute-optimal allocation, in a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that transformer symbolic regression follows predictable power-law scaling with compute in validation loss and solved rate. A token-to-parameter ratio of about 15 is optimal in their regime, rising slightly with compute, and optimal batch size and learning rate grow with model size.
record.recipe_differences: This is a symbolic-regression scaling study, not a language-model replication. It uses a custom synthetic-expression dataset and encoder-decoder transformer pipeline, sweeps model sizes and training settings, and fits trends across compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that optimal batch size and learning rate vary with model size; it also reports a slight increase in the optimal token-to-parameter ratio with compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Compute-optimal batch size and learning rate both grow with model size: BS = 0.004·N^0.597 and LR = 1.4e-6·N^0.356. The upward learning-rate trend contrasts with LLM findings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal training hyperparameters (batch size, learning rate) scale as power laws of model size, with task-dependent direction.

record.problems: The authors state that training used single-seed runs, the compute range is limited, extrapolations beyond it are unverified, and the expression domain is restricted to at most two variables and small integer constants. Evaluation metrics are averaged over three evaluation seeds, but no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: The full result table reports 25 runs and separate values for Accsolved, AccR2 > 0.99, and final validation loss. These per-run entries are not extracted individually; the aggregate scaling results in Figures 3, 7, and 8 and the compute-optimal fits in Figure 6 capture the findings relevant to the tested versions.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss. No separate loss-vs-parameters or loss-vs-tokens law with the other quantities non-bottlenecked.
There is a projection to 3.8e21 FLOPs, but it is never checked against larger runs; the authors call it unverified.
Depth and width are scaled together; there is no comparison of shapes at fixed parameter count.
No downstream language-model tasks. The solved rate is this task's own metric and is recorded under V5.
Fitting choices, parameter counting and schedules are not compared, and no curvature analysis is done.
Only symbolic regression is covered (two variables, integer constants). No image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.

missing.what: Per-model-size results on varying token-to-parameter ratio: loss and accuracy improve monotonically with tokens at each fixed size, e.g. 93M loss from 0.251 to 0.105. These bear on V5 for data scaling at fixed size and are declared in rows_left_out only as aggregate.

record.verdict_notes: This is a workshop paper. Training uses single seeds, with means over three evaluation seeds, and no uncertainty is reported. The compute span is under four orders of magnitude. The power-law form is assumed, not compared against alternatives. Exponent minus signs were lost in the text extraction. Linking R4–R6 to V3 treats the allocation claim as task-general; a strict reading of V3 as language-model-only would move these rows to V5.

versions.untested_parts: The models are for symbolic regression, not language models, and the study does not test loss scaling separately against parameters or tokens while holding the other quantities non-bottlenecked.
The study fits scaling trends and gives a projected solved rate at higher compute, but does not test predictions from small runs against observed runs orders of magnitude larger.
Tests compute-optimal parameters and expression-token counts in this symbolic-regression setup, not the corresponding allocation for language models or across a broader range of compute.
Model sizes vary architectural dimensions together; there is no controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests transformer symbolic regression only; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study reports symbolic-regression task metrics, not downstream language-model task performance or its relationship to pretraining loss.
It does not compare fitting choices or parameter-counting methods, test whether curves bend away from power laws, or show that published language-model laws disagree.

rows.subject: Five symbolic-regression transformers (aggregate scaling analysis)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to final validation loss across training compute on the Pareto front.

conditions.value: three orders of magnitude; plotted runs span approximately 10^16–10^19 FLOPs
symbolic-regression expressions with at most two variables

rows.measure: Final validation loss versus training compute
rows.value: Authors report a power-law fit; Figure 7 displays coefficient 1668.347 and exponent 0.218, but the exponent sign is unclear in the extracted figure text. The paper states that loss decreases with compute.
rows.note: The figure and text describe a decreasing validation-loss trend. The extracted fit notation appears to omit or obscure the exponent sign.
rows.check: The extracted fit 'C 0.218' has lost its minus sign. Loss falls with compute, from 0.55 to 0.105 in Table 2, so the exponent is about -0.218. The value should state this.

rows.subject: Five symbolic-regression transformers (aggregate scaling analysis)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to the perfect-solved ratio across training compute on the Pareto front.

conditions.value: test split; mean over three evaluation seeds

rows.value: Approximately 0.03 at the lowest compute budget and 0.6 at the highest; the paper reports power-law scaling. It projects 0.8 at 3.8×10^21 FLOPs.
rows.note: The fit is shown for 1 − Accsolved; the paper describes the solved ratio as increasing with compute.
rows.check: The value should give the Figure 3 fit on 1 − Accsolved: 94.742·C^-0.124 (sign lost in extraction). The 0.8 projection at 3.8×10^21 FLOPs is an unverified extrapolation, not an observed result.

rows.subject: Five symbolic-regression transformers (aggregate scaling analysis)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to the test expression ratio with R2 > 0.99 across training compute.

conditions.value: test split; mean over three evaluation seeds

rows.value: Authors report power-law scaling; the displayed fit gives coefficient 11055.328 and exponent 0.264, with the exponent sign unclear in the extracted figure text.
rows.note: The text says this metric follows power-law scaling and improves faster than the exact solved rate.
rows.check: The exponent sign was lost in extraction. The Figure 8 axis label says AccR2>0.99, but the coefficient and the decreasing axis suggest the fit is on 1 − AccR2>0.99 with exponent about -0.264. The value should say so.

rows.subject: Five symbolic-regression transformers (compute-optimal Pareto front)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to compute-optimal parameter count as a function of compute.
rows.note: The authors report a power-law fit to the compute-optimal parameter count.
rows.check: Valid only for symbolic regression with encoder-decoder FLOPs counted on feed-forward parameters. The fit rests on single-seed runs over about 4.5e15–1.5e19 FLOPs.

rows.subject: Five symbolic-regression transformers (compute-optimal Pareto front)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to compute-optimal expression-token count as a function of compute.
rows.note: The authors report a power-law fit to the compute-optimal dataset size.
rows.check: Same caveat as R4. The 'tokens' are expression (output) tokens, not input tokens.

rows.subject: Five symbolic-regression transformers (compute-optimal Pareto front)
rows.operation_detail: Compare the fitted compute-optimal token and parameter scaling trends.
rows.value: Approximately 15 in the studied compute regime, with a slight upward trend as compute increases.
rows.note: The paper says expression-token count scales slightly faster than parameter count.
rows.check: The exponents 0.445 and 0.555 imply a slowly rising token-to-parameter ratio. That is close to Hoffmann-style equal growth, with data slightly faster, and opposite to Kaplan's model-faster split. 'Partial' is relative to a stable equal split.
